quote.translation: The predicate or consequent is always inherent in the subject or antecedent (Semper praedicatum seu consequens inest subjecto seu antecedenti), and inherence (inesse) is nothing other than identity (idem esse), so that groundedness is, in the end, rooted in identity.

regions.text: いつたい異理の橙明は「理由なくしては何物もない」いふ理由律によるのである。理由律が妥営しないとすれば、ブプリオリに證明の出來ない異理があるといふことになる。

quote.translation: The proof of any truth rests, after all, on the law of ground, that "nothing is without a ground".

regions.text: そのやうな異理は同一性へ解體されない眞理を意味する。しかしそれは兵理の性質に反する。興理は現にであるにせよ暗にであるにせよともかくも常に同一的である（Alioqniveritasdaretur,quaenonpotestprobariapriori,seuquaenonresolvereturmidenticas,quodestcontramaturamveritatis,quaesempervelexpressevelimpliciteidenticacst）。

quote.translation: If the law of ground did not hold, there would be truths that could not be proved a priori, which is to say truths that could not be resolved into identity, and this is contrary to the nature of truth, since truth, whether explicitly or implicitly, is always identical (Alioqui veritas daretur, quae non potest probari a priori, seu quae non resolveretur in identicas, quod est contra naturam veritatis, quae semper vel expresse vel implicite identica est).

quote.translation: Émile Meyerson likewise points out that the law of ground is based on the law of identity: "This conviction of rationality, this conviction of necessary connection, has its origin solely in the reduction to the identity that exists between antecedent and consequent" (Émile Meyerson, Du cheminement de la Pensée, I. 1931, p. 55).
